description: High school students interested in space and rockets.
summary: Mission Control: Mars Explorer is a free browser-based simulation game in which students become the mission director for a Mars science orbiter. Students build a spacecraft by selecting the platform, solar panels, batteries, radio, engines, scientific instruments, orbit, and launch vehicle, and each selection affects the mass, power, delta-V, data downlink rate, and cost. An automatic GO/NO-GO launch evaluation filters out impossible designs and states why. Students then launch their design, cruise to Mars on a realistic minimum-energy transfer orbit, fire their engines to reach Mars orbit, and perform 360 days (sols) of scientific investigation while dealing with equipment problems, dust storms, and scientific discoveries. All the physics is real, but simple enough for high school students: inverse square sunlight, rocket equation, orbit periods, battery energy conservation through eclipses and limited communication ranges based on the values found in NASA’s Mars Fact Sheet. A ten-step tutorial and a score of 100 teach each player during each mission. We want to demonstrate that space mission design is an interconnected systems problem, not just a parts list, and we have done this in a format usable anywhere as a free Code.org Game Lab game.
details:
What it does. Mission Control: Mars Explorer is a single-player strategy and simulation game about designing and operating a Mars orbiter. The player is the mission director of a fictional space agency. The goal is to map the Martian surface, study the atmosphere and look for evidence of past water, while keeping the spacecraft alive for a planned 360-sol mission.

How it works. The game runs through the full life of a mission:

  1. Difficulty and briefing. Easy, Normal and Hard change the budget, the required engineering margin (0, 5, or 10%), ground-station contact time and how often and how hard events hit.
  2. Spacecraft builder. Nine tabs: platform, solar arrays, battery, communications, propulsion, science instruments, Mars orbit, launch vehicle and upgrades. Every click shows its exact effect, for example “+30 kg, +13 MC, dV −40 m/s”.
  3. Engineering dashboard. Eight live readouts: budget, launch mass, power, eclipse energy, data storage, downlink, delta-v and estimated lifetime. Each explains its formula and any problem using the player’s own numbers.
  4. GO/NO-GO launch review. Mission-control stations report one by one. Launch is blocked until every required system is GO, and each failure states why and how to fix it.
  5. Launch, cruise and orbit insertion. Launch success depends on the launcher’s reliability and spare capacity. The cruise follows a real Hohmann transfer, with Earth and Mars moving at their true average speeds and decisions about course corrections and an engine test. At Mars, the player either trusts an autonomous burn or times it by hand, because Earth is about 13 light-minutes away. Too little delta-v means a degraded orbit or a fly-by.
  6. Science operations. The player switches between SCIENCE, TRANSMIT, CONSERVE and MAINTAIN modes. The battery charges and drains orbit by orbit through Mars’s shadow, and the recorder can overflow. Downlink falls with Earth–Mars distance, and a solar-conjunction blackout happens when the planets’ real positions put the Sun between them. Eleven events (array degradation, radio outages, instrument faults, storage failures, reaction-wheel problems, battery cell loss, propellant leaks, dust storms, discoveries, aerobraking heating and solar flares) pause the game and offer two or three choices, each with a cost and a short lesson.
  7. Mission report. A transparent score out of 100 (40 science, 25 reliability, 20 efficiency, 15 completion), a list of accomplishments and failures, and specific recommendations. Players earn R&D points for upgrades and can retry or redesign immediately.

The science. The game uses real relationships with simplified, clearly labelled numbers:

  • inverse-square sunlight: about 43% of Earth’s at 1.52 AU, matching NASA’s value of 0.431;
  • the rocket equation;
  • circular orbit periods from Mars’s gravitational parameter;
  • eclipse geometry;
  • energy = power × time for battery sizing;
  • Kepler’s equation for the transfer orbit;
  • data rate × contact time, falling with distance squared;
  • light-time delays of 3 to 22 minutes.

Spacecraft parts, prices and launchers are fictional. Every value in the code is tagged [PHYS], [APPROX] or [GAME] so students can tell real physics from game design.

Benefits and intended impact. Students usually meet spacecraft as lists of parts. This game makes them feel that adding one instrument changes power, arrays, mass, propellant, the rocket and the budget all at once. It runs in any browser for free with no installs, so any classroom with Code.org access can use it. A 10-step interactive tutorial covers what an orbiter does, mass and delta-v, launch capacity, solar power and distance, batteries, data, communications, orbit insertion, reliability and trade-offs. Easy mode opens the tutorial automatically.

Tools, languages and software.

  • JavaScript (ES5) in Code.org Game Lab. All graphics are pixel art drawn by the code itself, with no image files.
    • a sweep of all 34,992 possible designs on every difficulty;
    • hundreds of simulated missions with random events;
    • edge cases such as the cheapest design, the heaviest design, battery depletion and communications failure.
  • A browser-based readability audit that measured every text label on more than 70 screen states and found no overlaps or clipping.
  • A Super Intelligence tool, Claude by Anthropic, which generated the code under the team’s direction. This is disclosed in the code, the README, the About screen and the slides.

Creativity.

  • A real GO/NO-GO poll as a teaching device.
  • Explanations that quote the player’s own numbers instead of generic errors.
  • A solar-conjunction blackout that emerges from orbital geometry rather than chance.
  • A manual orbit-insertion mode that teaches why real burns are autonomous.
  • Scoring that only credits science data that actually reaches Earth.

Factors we considered.

  • Scientific honesty: real relationships, documented simplifications, no invented NASA specifications.
  • Accessibility: free, browser-based, a LITE graphics mode for slow school computers, readable text sizes and mouse-only play.
  • Balance: many different designs can score well, and difficulty changes real variables.
  • Performance limits inside Game Lab’s interpreter.
  • Transparent disclosure of SI use.
  • No NASA logos or branding.
